title: Ἀθήνη καὶ ὁ Κρητικὸς μῦθος
titleEn: Athena and the Cretan Tale — Odyssey 13.217–328
about: Odysseus counts his gifts on the shore, sure that the Phaeacians have cheated him, and mourns for a homeland he does not know. Athena comes to him disguised as a young herdsman. He greets her as a stranger and asks where he is, and she tells him it is Ithaca, a name known even at Troy. Glad but wary, he answers with an invented tale: a Cretan who killed a king’s son over Trojan spoil and was carried off course by Phoenician sailors who then robbed him. Athena smiles, takes a woman’s shape and teases him for his tricks, since the two of them are alike in cunning. She says she will hide his goods with him and warns that he must bear his troubles in silence. Odysseus, still doubtful, begs her to tell him whether this is truly his own country.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν τρίποδας περικαλλέας ἠδὲ λέβητας
ἠρίθμει καὶ χρυσὸν ὑφαντά τε εἵματα καλά.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, the tripods very fair and the cauldrons
he counted, and the gold, and the woven garments, fine.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and counted the very fair tripods and the cauldrons, and the gold, and the fine woven clothing.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes Odysseus’s speech of 200–216 and turns back to the narrator; the goods he feared were stolen are now checked one by one. τρίποδας and λέβητας are accusative plurals: a τρίπους is a three-legged stand or vessel, a λέβης a cauldron, both treasured as gifts. περικαλλέας is ‘very fair’, with περι- as an intensive ‘exceedingly’. ἠρίθμει is the imperfect of ἀριθμέω ‘count’, with -ει for -εε, so ‘he went on counting’. ὑφαντά is the verbal adjective of ὑφαίνω ‘weave’, and εἵματα is the plural of εἷμα ‘garment’. The paragraph starts here.

sentences.t: τῶν μὲν ἄρ’ οὔ τι πόθει·
sentences.l: Of these indeed then not at all did he feel longing;
sentences.i: Yet for these things he felt no longing;
sentences.n: τῶν is the genitive of the pronoun, ‘for these’, and it is governed by πόθει, the imperfect of ποθέω ‘long for, miss’, which takes the genitive; the form has no augment and is contracted from πόθεε. οὔ τι is ‘not at all’. μὲν … ὁ δέ sets this against the next unit: he missed none of the treasure, but he did mourn his land. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ὀδύρετο πατρίδα γαῖαν
ἑρπύζων παρὰ θῖνα πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης,
πόλλ’ ὀλοφυρόμενος.
sentences.l:
but he mourned the fatherland,
creeping along the shore of the much-roaring sea,
lamenting much.
sentences.i: but he mourned for his fatherland as he crept along the shore of the loud-roaring sea, lamenting greatly.
sentences.n: ὁ is ‘he’, Odysseus, and ὀδύρετο is the imperfect middle of ὀδύρομαι ‘mourn, lament’, with πατρίδα γαῖαν ‘fatherland’ as its object. ἑρπύζων is from ἑρπύζω, a lengthened form of ἕρπω ‘creep, move slowly’. θῖνα is the accusative of θίς ‘shore, beach’. πολυφλοίσβοιο is a genitive in -οιο from πολύφλοισβος ‘much-roaring’, with φλοῖσβος the noise of surf breaking. ὀλοφυρόμενος is the present participle of ὀλοφύρομαι ‘lament’, and πόλλ’ is the neuter plural used as an adverb, ‘much’. The unit ends at the full stop in mid-line 221.

sentences.t:
σχεδόθεν δέ οἱ ἦλθεν Ἀθήνη,
ἀνδρὶ δέμας εἰκυῖα νέῳ, ἐπιβώτορι μήλων,
παναπάλῳ, οἷοί τε ἀνάκτων παῖδες ἔασι,
δίπτυχον ἀμφ’ ὤμοισιν ἔχουσ’ εὐεργέα λώπην·
sentences.l:
and near at hand came to him Athena,
to a man in body likened, a young one, a herder of flocks,
very tender, such as lords’ sons are,
a double, well-wrought cloak about her shoulders having;
sentences.i: Athena came close to him, in the body of a young man, a keeper of flocks, very delicate, such as the sons of lords are, with a well-made double cloak about her shoulders;
sentences.n: Athena comes to Odysseus disguised, and the Greek still calls her ‘she’: εἰκυῖα ‘likened’ and ἔχουσ’ ‘having’ are feminine participles, though the body she has taken is a young man’s. οἱ is ‘to him’, and σχεδόθεν ‘from near by’ has the suffix -θεν. δέμας is an accusative of respect, ‘in body’, and ἀνδρὶ … νέῳ is the dative after εἰκυῖα, the feminine perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’. ἐπιβώτορι is ἐπιβώτωρ ‘herdsman’, with μήλων ‘of flocks’ (sheep and goats). παναπάλῳ is παν- ‘very’ and ἁπαλός ‘tender’, soft-skinned; οἷοί τε ἀνάκτων παῖδες ἔασι ‘such as lords’ sons are’ explains it (ἔασι is εἰσί). δίπτυχον is ‘double’, a cloak folded in two; εὐεργέα is ‘well-wrought’ and λώπην ‘cloak’. ἀμφ’ ὤμοισιν is ἀμφὶ ὤμοισιν ‘about her shoulders’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 224.

sentences.t: ποσσὶ δ’ ὑπὸ λιπαροῖσι πέδιλ’ ἔχε, χερσὶ δ’ ἄκοντα.
sentences.l: and under her sleek feet sandals she had, and in her hands a javelin.
sentences.i: On her sleek feet she wore sandals, and in her hands she held a javelin.
sentences.n: ποσσί is the dative plural of πούς ‘foot’ (Attic ποσί), with ὑπό ‘under’, and λιπαροῖσι is ‘sleek’, the shine of skin rubbed with oil. πέδιλ’ is πέδιλα ‘sandals’, and ἔχε is the imperfect of ἔχω without augment (Attic εἶχε). With χερσί ‘in her hands’ the same verb is understood. ἄκοντα is the accusative of ἄκων ‘javelin’, which a herdsman would carry.

sentences.t:
τὴν δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς γήθησεν ἰδὼν καὶ ἐναντίος ἦλθε,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
Odysseus rejoiced, seeing her, and face to face he came,
and, lifting his voice, to her winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Odysseus was glad when he saw her, and went to meet her, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to her:
sentences.n: Odysseus is glad to see a living person at last. τήν is ‘her’, the object of ἰδών, and γήθησεν is the aorist of γηθέω ‘rejoice’. ἐναντίος ‘face to face’ agrees with Ὀδυσεύς, whose single σ is a metrical variant of Ὀδυσσεύς (line 250). Line 227 is a whole-line formula for the moment before a speech: φωνήσας ‘lifting his voice’ is the participle of φωνέω, μιν is ‘her’, ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’, and προσηύδα ‘spoke to’ is the imperfect of προσαυδάω. It returns unchanged at 253 and, with a feminine participle, at 290.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλ’, ἐπεί σε πρῶτα κιχάνω τῷδ’ ἐνὶ χώρῳ,
χαῖρέ τε καὶ μή μοί τι κακῷ νόῳ ἀντιβολήσαις,
ἀλλὰ σάω μὲν ταῦτα, σάω δ’ ἐμέ·
sentences.i: “Friend, since you are the first I find in this place, welcome — and may you not meet me with any ill intent, but keep these goods safe, and me too;
sentences.n: This is Odysseus’s opening appeal, and its point is a request for protection. ὦ φίλ’ is ὦ φίλε ‘O friend’. πρῶτα is an adverbial accusative, ‘first’: the stranger is the first person he has met here. κιχάνω is the present of κιχάνω ‘come upon, find’. χαῖρε is the imperative of χαίρω ‘rejoice’, the common greeting. ἀντιβολήσαις is the aorist optative of ἀντιβολέω ‘meet, encounter’, and after μή it is a wish, ‘may you not meet me with a wicked mind’; κακῷ νόῳ is a dative of manner. σάω is the imperative of σαόω ‘keep safe, save’ (Attic σῴζω): the first σάω has ταῦτα ‘these things’, the goods beside him, as its object, the second has ἐμέ ‘me’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 230.

sentences.t:
σοὶ γὰρ ἐγώ γε
εὔχομαι ὥς τε θεῷ καί σευ φίλα γούναθ’ ἱκάνω.
sentences.l:
for to you I, at least,
make my prayer as to a god, and to your dear knees I come.
sentences.i: for to you I make my prayer, as to a god, and I have come to your knees.
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for the request. σοί goes with εὔχομαι, which with the dative means ‘I pray to’, the word used for a prayer to a god; γε follows ἐγώ and stresses it, ‘I at least’. ὥς τε θεῷ is ‘as to a god’, with the enclitic τε after ὥς. σευ is the epic genitive of σύ (Attic σου), γούναθ’ is γούνατα ‘knees’ elided, and φίλα ‘dear’ is the ordinary epithet for what belongs to the person addressed. ἱκάνω is ‘I come to’. To come to someone’s knees is the posture of a suppliant.

sentences.t: καί μοι τοῦτ’ ἀγόρευσον ἐτήτυμον, ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδῶ·
sentences.l: And tell me this truly, so that I may know it well:
sentences.i: And tell me this truly, so that I may know it well:
sentences.n: ἀγόρευσον is the aorist imperative of ἀγορεύω ‘speak, tell’, and ἐτήτυμον is the adjective used as an adverb, ‘truly’. ὄφρα ‘so that’ takes the subjunctive εἰδῶ ‘I may know’ (of οἶδα), and ἐῢ is the short form of εὖ ‘well’. The question comes next.

sentences.t: τίς γῆ, τίς δῆμος, τίνες ἀνέρες ἐγγεγάασιν;
sentences.l: What land, what people, what men are born in it?
sentences.i: What land is this, what people, and what men live here?
sentences.n: Three questions in one line, with ‘is’ left out of the first two: τίς γῆ, τίς δῆμος ‘what land, what people (or district)?’. ἐγγεγάασιν is the perfect of ἐγγίγνομαι, with γεγάασι for γεγόνασι, so ‘have been born in’ and hence ‘live in’. ἀνέρες is the epic nominative plural of ἀνήρ (Attic ἄνδρες).

sentences.t:
ἦ πού τις νήσων εὐδείελος, ἦέ τις ἀκτὴ
κεῖθ’ ἁλὶ κεκλιμένη ἐριβώλακος ἠπείροιο;
sentences.l:
Is it perhaps some clear-seen one of the islands, or some shore
that lies inclined to the sea, of the rich-soiled mainland?”
sentences.i: Is it perhaps one of the clear-seen islands, or some shore of the rich-soiled mainland that slopes down to the sea?”
sentences.n: The last question gives him two choices: an island or the coast of a mainland. ἦ πού is ‘is it perhaps’, and ἦέ is ἠέ ‘or’. νήσων with τις is partitive, ‘some one of the islands’. εὐδείελος ‘clear-seen’ is the traditional gloss; its exact sense is disputed. ἀκτή is ‘headland, shore’. κεῖθ’ is κεῖται ‘lies’, ἁλί is the dative of ἅλς ‘sea’, and κεκλιμένη is the perfect middle participle of κλίνω ‘lean’, so ‘lies sloping to the sea’. ἐριβώλακος ‘rich-soiled’ is ἐρι- ‘very’ and βῶλος ‘clod’, and ἠπείροιο is the genitive of ἤπειρος ‘mainland’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.i: Then the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: This is a reply-formula, and it names the speaker, so the reader knows who the ‘young man’ is though Odysseus does not. τόν is ‘him’. αὖτε ‘in turn’ is the word that marks an answer, and προσέειπε is the uncontracted aorist of προσεῖπον ‘addressed’. θεά ‘goddess’ stands in front of the fixed phrase γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη, whose epithet means ‘gleaming-eyed’ (the second half is from ὤψ ‘eye, face’; the first half is of disputed meaning, ‘gleaming’ or ‘owl’).

sentences.t:
νήπιός εἰς, ὦ ξεῖν’, ἢ τηλόθεν εἰλήλουθας,
εἰ δὴ τήνδε τε γαῖαν ἀνείρεαι.
sentences.l:
“A fool you are, stranger, or from far off you have come,
if indeed about this land you ask.
sentences.i: “You are a fool, stranger, or else you have come from far away, if you really are asking about this land.
sentences.n: Athena’s answer begins with a rebuke that Odysseus is meant to take as plain surprise. νήπιος is ‘foolish’, literally ‘childish’. εἰς is the Ionic second person singular of εἰμί, ‘you are’ (Attic εἶ), not the preposition. ὦ ξεῖν’ is ὦ ξεῖνε ‘stranger’. τηλόθεν ‘from far’ has the suffix -θεν, and εἰλήλουθας is the perfect of ἔρχομαι ‘you have come’ (Attic ἐλήλυθας). In εἰ δὴ … ἀνείρεαι, ἀνείρεαι ‘you ask about’ (ἀνείρομαι, the epic form of ἀνέρομαι) takes the accusative τήνδε … γαῖαν, and εἰ δή is ‘if indeed’. The unit ends at the full stop in line 238.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι λίην
οὕτω νώνυμός ἐστιν·
sentences.l:
nor at all too much
so nameless is it;
sentences.i: it is not so very nameless;
sentences.n: νώνυμος is a form of ἀνώνυμος ‘nameless’, from ὄνομα ‘name’ with a negative prefix; the idea of the name returns in ὄνομ’ at line 248. λίην is the Ionic form of λίαν ‘too much, very’, and οὐδέ τι λίην οὕτω together mean ‘not at all so very’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 239.

sentences.t:
ἴσασι δέ μιν μάλα πολλοί,
ἠμὲν ὅσοι ναίουσι πρὸς ἠῶ τ’ ἠέλιόν τε,
ἠδ’ ὅσσοι μετόπισθε ποτὶ ζόφον ἠερόεντα.
sentences.l:
but know it very many,
both as many as dwell toward the dawn and the sun,
and as many as behind, toward the misty gloom.
sentences.i: Very many people know it, both those who live toward the dawn and the sun and those who live behind, toward the misty gloom.
sentences.n: ἴσασι is ‘they know’, the third plural of οἶδα, and μιν is ‘it’, the land. ἠμέν … ἠδ’ is ‘both … and’, and ὅσοι … ὅσσοι ‘as many as’. πρὸς ἠῶ τ’ ἠέλιόν τε ‘toward the dawn and the sun’ is the east. μετόπισθε ‘behind’ points the other way, toward ζόφος, the gloom of the west, and ἠερόεντα ‘misty’ comes from ἀήρ ‘mist’. ποτί is πρός. The two halves together mean ‘everyone, everywhere’.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι μὲν τρηχεῖα καὶ οὐχ ἱππήλατός ἐστιν,
οὐδὲ λίην λυπρή, ἀτὰρ οὐδ’ εὐρεῖα τέτυκται.
sentences.l:
Truly, rough it is, and not fit for driving horses,
nor too poor, yet neither broad has it been made.
sentences.i: It is rough, and not fit for driving horses, though it is not very poor, but neither is it broad.
sentences.n: ἦ τοι μέν is ‘truly indeed’, and what follows is a frank description of the island’s limits. τρηχεῖα is ‘rough’ (Attic τραχεῖα). ἱππήλατος ‘fit for driving horses’ is ἵππος ‘horse’ with ἐλαύνω ‘drive’: ground too broken for chariots. λίην λυπρή is ‘too poor’, with λυπρός ‘mean, scanty’. τέτυκται is the perfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’, ‘has been made’, and so ‘is’. ἀτὰρ οὐδ’ is ‘but not … either’.

sentences.t:
ἐν μὲν γάρ οἱ σῖτος ἀθέσφατος, ἐν δέ τε οἶνος
γίγνεται·
sentences.l:
for in it indeed grain immense, and in it too wine
grows;
sentences.i: for grain grows there in immense quantity, and wine too;
sentences.n: The ἐν … ἐν lists what the land produces, and οἱ ‘in it’ is a dative of the land. The one verb γίγνεται ‘comes to be, grows’ serves both subjects. ἀθέσφατος is ‘immense’; it is traditionally taken as ‘not spoken by a god’, that is ‘beyond telling’, but its sense is not certain. τε after δέ is a small particle of addition. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 245.

sentences.t: αἰεὶ δ’ ὄμβρος ἔχει τεθαλυῖά τ’ ἐέρση·
sentences.l: and always rain holds it, and flourishing dew;
sentences.i: and rain is always upon it, and flourishing dew;
sentences.n: ἔχει has ὄμβρος ‘rain’ as subject, and its object, the land, is understood: ‘rain always has it’. τεθαλυῖα is the feminine perfect participle of θάλλω ‘bloom, thrive’, ‘flourishing’, and ἐέρση is the epic form of ἕρση ‘dew’ with an extra ε. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: αἰγίβοτος δ’ ἀγαθὴ καὶ βούβοτος·
sentences.l: goat-pasturing it is good, and cattle-pasturing;
sentences.i: it is good land for pasturing goats and cattle;
sentences.n: αἰγίβοτος ‘goat-pasturing’ (αἴξ ‘goat’) and βούβοτος ‘cattle-pasturing’ (βοῦς ‘ox’) are compounds built on the root of βόσκω ‘feed, pasture’. ἀγαθή ‘good’ has its verb understood. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 246.

sentences.t:
ἔστι μὲν ὕλη
παντοίη, ἐν δ’ ἀρδμοὶ ἐπηετανοὶ παρέασι.
sentences.l:
there is indeed woodland
of every kind, and in it never-failing watering-places are at hand.
sentences.i: There is woodland of every kind, and never-failing watering-places are at hand.
sentences.n: ἔστι ‘there is’ opens the unit, and παρέασι is πάρεισι ‘are at hand’. ὕλη is ‘woodland, timber’ and παντοίη ‘of every kind’. ἀρδμοί are places for stock to drink, from ἄρδω ‘water’. ἐπηετανοί is ‘never-failing’; the sense is only approximately known, and the traditional gloss is ‘abundant, lasting all year’.

sentences.t:
τῷ τοι, ξεῖν’, Ἰθάκης γε καὶ ἐς Τροίην ὄνομ’ ἵκει,
τήν περ τηλοῦ φασὶν Ἀχαιΐδος ἔμμεναι αἴης.
sentences.l:
Therefore, stranger, of Ithaca even to Troy the name has come,
which they say is far from the Achaean land.”
sentences.i: So, stranger, the name of Ithaca has reached even Troy, which they say is far from the Achaean land.”
sentences.n: This is the answer to Odysseus’s question: the name of the land is Ithaca, given as a name that has travelled even to Troy. τῷ is an old instrumental of the pronoun, ‘therefore’, and τοι is ‘to you’. Ἰθάκης is a genitive depending on ὄνομ’ (ὄνομα). γε … καί is ‘even’, and ἵκει is the present of ἵκω ‘reach’. τήν περ is the relative ‘which indeed’, and its antecedent is Τροίην ‘Troy’. τηλοῦ ‘far’ takes the genitive Ἀχαιΐδος … αἴης, ‘from the Achaean land’, with αἴη the Ionic form of αἶα ‘land’, and ἔμμεναι is the infinitive ‘to be’. Athena’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, γήθησεν δὲ πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
χαίρων ᾗ γαίῃ πατρωΐῃ, ὥς οἱ ἔειπε
Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη, κούρη Διὸς, αἰγιόχοιο·
sentences.i: So she spoke, and much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus rejoiced, glad of his own father’s land, as Pallas Athena, the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus, had told him;
sentences.n: Narration resumes. ὣς φάτο is ‘so she spoke’, and the first line is a name-formula that fills the verse: πολύτλας ‘much-enduring’ and δῖος ‘heavenly’ stand with the name. χαίρων takes the dative ᾗ γαίῃ, where ᾗ is the possessive ‘his own’ and πατρωΐῃ is the dative of πατρώϊος ‘of his father’. ὥς οἱ ἔειπε is ‘as she told him’, with ἔειπε for εἶπε, and the narrator repeats the speaker’s full name and descent. αἰγιόχοιο ‘aegis-bearing’ is the epithet of Zeus; its meaning is disputed, the aegis being a divine shield or mantle and the second half read as ‘holding’. Παλλάς is a name whose meaning is also disputed. Ἀθηναίη is the Ionic form of Ἀθηναία. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 252.

sentences.t: καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l: And, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: And lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: The speech formula of line 227 repeats unchanged, with μιν ‘him’: Odysseus is again the speaker. This time the narrator has already named Athena, and Odysseus has not recognised her, and what follows is a lie.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ὅ γ’ ἀληθέα εἶπε, πάλιν δ’ ὅ γε λάζετο μῦθον,
αἰεὶ ἐνὶ στήθεσσι νόον πολυκερδέα νωμῶν·
sentences.l:
But not true things did he say, back again he took the word,
always in his breast a mind of many gains turning over:
sentences.i: But he did not tell the truth: he took the word back, always turning over in his breast a mind alert to every advantage:
sentences.n: The narrator warns his audience that the story to come is false. οὐδ’ ὅ γ’ ἀληθέα εἶπε is ‘but he did not speak true things’: ἀληθέα is the uncontracted neuter plural of ἀληθής, and ὅ γε is ‘he’. πάλιν … λάζετο μῦθον is ‘he took the word back’: λάζετο is the aorist middle of λάζομαι ‘seize’. The idiom is taken to mean that he turned his words away from the truth, but its exact sense is not certain. πολυκερδέα ‘of many gains’ is the epithet of νόον ‘mind’, built on κέρδος ‘gain, advantage, cunning’, the root also of κερδαλέος in 291 and κέρδε’ in 297. νωμῶν is from νωμάω ‘turn over, ply’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 255.

sentences.t:
πυνθανόμην Ἰθάκης γε καὶ ἐν Κρήτῃ εὐρείῃ,
τηλοῦ ὑπὲρ πόντου·
sentences.l:
“I heard of Ithaca, even in broad Crete,
far over the sea;
sentences.i: “I heard of Ithaca, even in broad Crete, far across the sea;
sentences.n: The false tale begins: he implies that he is a Cretan, an identity the story fills in at 260. πυνθανόμην is the imperfect of πυνθάνομαι ‘learn by inquiry, hear’, and takes the genitive Ἰθάκης. γε … καί is ‘even’. Κρήτῃ εὐρείῃ is a dative: εὐρείῃ is Ionic for εὐρείᾳ, ‘broad’, a fixed epithet of the island. τηλοῦ ὑπὲρ πόντου is ‘far over the sea’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 257.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ εἰλήλουθα καὶ αὐτὸς
χρήμασι σὺν τοίσδεσσι·
sentences.l:
and now I have come, I myself also,
with these goods;
sentences.i: and now I have come here myself as well, with these goods;
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ ‘and now’ turns from what he heard to what he did. εἰλήλουθα is the perfect of ἔρχομαι, ‘I have come’, the first person of the form in line 237. καὶ αὐτός is ‘myself also’. τοίσδεσσι is τοῖσδε, the dative plural of ὅδε ‘this’, lengthened with -εσσι, and χρήμασι ‘goods’ are the treasure on the shore. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 258.

sentences.t:
λιπὼν δ’ ἔτι παισὶ τοσαῦτα
φεύγω, ἐπεὶ φίλον υἷα κατέκτανον Ἰδομενῆος,
Ὀρσίλοχον πόδας ὠκύν, ὃς ἐν Κρήτῃ εὐρείῃ
ἀνέρας ἀλφηστὰς νίκα ταχέεσσι πόδεσσιν,
sentences.l:
and leaving behind besides as much to my children
I am in flight, since I killed the dear son of Idomeneus,
Orsilochus, swift in feet, who in broad Crete
gain-winning men outdid with quick feet,
sentences.i: and, leaving as much besides to my children, I am in flight, since I killed the dear son of Idomeneus, Orsilochus, swift of foot, who in broad Crete beat the men who earn their living, with his quick feet,
sentences.n: A detail of a false life: a man with children at home, driven into exile by a killing. ἔτι … τοσαῦτα is ‘as much besides’, and παισί is the dative plural of παῖς ‘child’. φεύγω is ‘I am in flight, I am an exile’. ἐπεὶ … κατέκτανον is ‘since I killed’, an aorist with its augment (κατ- + ἔκτανον). Ἰδομενῆος is the Ionic genitive of Ἰδομενεύς ‘Idomeneus’. Ὀρσίλοχον πόδας ὠκύν is ‘swift as to feet’, with πόδας an accusative of respect. ἀλφηστάς ‘men who earn their living’ is of uncertain meaning, either from ἀλφάνω ‘find, earn’ or from an old guess ‘grain-eating’; the translation takes the first. νίκα is the imperfect of νικάω ‘beat, surpass’, without augment, and ταχέεσσι πόδεσσιν is a dative with -εσσι. The unit stops at a comma because the sentence runs on to line 266.

sentences.t:
οὕνεκά με στερέσαι τῆς ληΐδος ἤθελε πάσης
Τρωϊάδος, τῆς εἵνεκ’ ἐγὼ πάθον ἄλγεα θυμῷ,
ἀνδρῶν τε πτολέμους ἀλεγεινά τε κύματα πείρων,
sentences.l:
because me to deprive of the spoil all
Trojan he wished, for whose sake I suffered pains in my heart,
the wars of men and grievous waves passing through,
sentences.i: because he wanted to deprive me of all the Trojan spoil, for the sake of which I suffered pains in my heart, making my way through the wars of men and the grievous waves,
sentences.n: This is the first of Odysseus’s two stated reasons for the killing, and it is his real history put to use: the spoil of Troy and the suffering for it. οὕνεκα is ‘because’, and στερέσαι is the aorist infinitive of στερέω ‘deprive’, with the genitive τῆς ληΐδος … πάσης Τρωϊάδος, ‘of all the Trojan spoil’; Τρωϊάδος is the feminine adjective ‘Trojan’. τῆς εἵνεκ’ is τῆς ἕνεκα ‘for whose sake’, and πάθον is the aorist of πάσχω ‘suffer’ without augment. ἀνδρῶν τε πτολέμους ἀλεγεινά τε κύματα πείρων is a stock verse: πείρων ‘passing through’ governs both accusatives, ‘the wars of men’ and ‘the grievous waves’. The unit stops at a comma, with a second reason in the next.

sentences.t:
οὕνεκ’ ἄρ’ οὐχ ᾧ πατρὶ χαριζόμενος θεράπευον
δήμῳ ἔνι Τρώων, ἀλλ’ ἄλλων ἦρχον ἑταίρων.
sentences.l:
because I was not serving his own father, gratifying him,
in the land of the Trojans, but of other companions I was the leader.
sentences.i: because I did not serve his father to gratify him in the land of the Trojans, but led other companions.
sentences.n: οὕνεκ’ ἄρ’ takes up the οὕνεκα of 262 for the second reason: the first was about the spoil, this one is about service. ᾧ is the possessive ‘his own’, so ᾧ πατρί is Orsilochus’s own father, Idomeneus. χαριζόμενος is ‘gratifying, doing a favour’, and θεράπευον is the imperfect of θεραπεύω ‘serve’. δήμῳ ἔνι Τρώων is ‘in the land of the Trojans’, with ἔνι for ἐν. ἄλλων ἑταίρων ἦρχον is ‘I led other companions’, with ἄρχω taking the genitive: men of his own, not Idomeneus’s.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ κατιόντα βάλον χαλκήρεϊ δουρὶ
ἀγρόθεν, ἐγγὺς ὁδοῖο λοχησάμενος σὺν ἑταίρῳ·
sentences.l:
Him indeed I, as he was coming down, struck with a bronze-fitted spear
from the field, near the road having lain in ambush with a companion;
sentences.i: I struck him with my bronze-fitted spear as he was coming back from the country, after lying in wait with a companion near the road;
sentences.n: τὸν μέν is ‘him’, Orsilochus. κατιόντα is the accusative participle of κάτειμι ‘come down’, here ‘coming back (from the fields)’. χαλκήρεϊ δουρί is the dative of δόρυ ‘spear’ with χαλκήρης ‘bronze-fitted’, tipped with bronze. βάλον is the aorist ‘I struck’, without augment. ἀγρόθεν ‘from the field’ has the suffix -θεν, and ἐγγὺς ὁδοῖο is ‘near the road’, with the genitive. λοχησάμενος is the aorist middle participle of λοχάω ‘lie in ambush’, from λόχος, and σὺν ἑταίρῳ ‘with a companion’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 268.

sentences.t:
νὺξ δὲ μάλα δνοφερὴ κάτεχ’ οὐρανόν, οὐδέ τις ἡμέας
ἀνθρώπων ἐνόησε, λάθον δέ ἑ θυμὸν ἀπούρας.
sentences.l:
and night very dark held down the sky, and not any
of men noticed us, and I escaped notice, having taken his life.
sentences.i: A very dark night held the sky, and no man noticed us; I took his life and escaped notice.
sentences.n: νύξ … κάτεχ’ οὐρανόν is ‘night held down the sky’: κάτεχ’ is κάτεχε, the imperfect of κατέχω without augment, and δνοφερή ‘dark’ comes from δνόφος ‘darkness’. οὐδέ τις ἡμέας ἀνθρώπων ἐνόησε is ‘not any of men noticed us’, with ἡμέας for ἡμᾶς and ἐνόησε ‘noticed’. λάθον is the aorist of λανθάνω without augment, ‘I escaped notice’, and ἑ is ‘him’. θυμὸν ἀπούρας is ‘having taken away his life’: ἀπούρας is the aorist participle of ἀπαυράω ‘take away’. θυμός is usually ‘heart, spirit’; with a verb of taking it is the life that leaves the body.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ τόν γε κατέκτανον ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
αὐτίκ’ ἐγὼν ἐπὶ νῆα κιὼν Φοίνικας ἀγαυοὺς
ἐλλισάμην, καί σφιν μενοεικέα ληΐδα δῶκα·
sentences.i: But when I had killed him with the sharp bronze, I went at once to a ship and begged the noble Phoenicians, and gave them satisfying spoil;
sentences.n: κατέκτανον ‘I had killed’ is the aorist of κατακτείνω, with its augment, as at 259. ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ ‘the sharp bronze’ names the weapon by its metal. ἐπὶ νῆα κιών is ‘going to a ship’, with κιών the participle of κίω ‘go’. Φοίνικας ἀγαυούς ‘noble Phoenicians’ is the object of ἐλλισάμην, the aorist of λίσσομαι ‘beg’. σφιν is ‘to them’, and μενοεικέα ‘satisfying’ is traditionally ‘fitting one’s desire’, from μένος in the sense of ‘desire’. ληΐδα is ‘spoil’, and δῶκα is the aorist of δίδωμι without augment. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 273.

sentences.t:
τούς μ’ ἐκέλευσα Πύλονδε καταστῆσαι καὶ ἐφέσσαι
ἢ εἰς Ἤλιδα δῖαν, ὅθι κρατέουσιν Ἐπειοί.
sentences.l:
and these I bade to Pylos to set me down and to land me
or to heavenly Elis, where the Epeans hold sway.
sentences.i: I bade them land me at Pylos and set me down there, or at heavenly Elis, where the Epeans hold sway.
sentences.n: τούς is ‘them’, the Phoenicians. ἐκέλευσα ‘I bade’ takes μ’ (με) as the object of the two aorist infinitives καταστῆσαι (from καθίστημι, ‘set down, bring to land’) and ἐφέσσαι (from ἐφίζω, ‘cause to sit, settle’); the two verbs overlap in sense, and together they mean ‘put me ashore’. Πύλονδε has the suffix -δε ‘to’, so ‘to Pylos’. Ἤλιδα δῖαν is ‘heavenly Elis’, with Ἤλιδα the accusative of Ἦλις. ὅθι is ‘where’, κρατέουσιν ‘hold sway’, and Ἐπειοί ‘Epeans’ are the people of Elis.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι σφέας κεῖθεν ἀπώσατο ἲς ἀνέμοιο
πόλλ’ ἀεκαζομένους, οὐδ’ ἤθελον ἐξαπατῆσαι.
sentences.l:
But truly them from there drove off the force of the wind,
much against their will, nor did they wish to deceive me.
sentences.i: But the force of the wind drove them away from there, much against their will, and they had no wish to deceive me.
sentences.n: The subject of ἤθελον is the Phoenicians: the form is the same for ‘I wished’ and ‘they wished’, but σφέας ‘them’ is the object of the first verb, and the sense is ‘nor did they wish to cheat me’. ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι is ‘but in fact’. ἀπώσατο is the aorist middle of ἀπωθέω ‘push away’, and ἲς ἀνέμοιο is ‘the force of the wind’, with a genitive in -οιο. ἀεκαζομένους is the participle of ἀεκάζομαι ‘be unwilling’, with πόλλ’ ‘much’. ἐξαπατῆσαι is the aorist infinitive of ἐξαπατάω ‘deceive completely’.

sentences.t: κεῖθεν δὲ πλαγχθέντες ἱκάνομεν ἐνθάδε νυκτός.
sentences.l: and from there, driven astray, we came here by night.
sentences.i: and so, driven off course from there, we came here by night.
sentences.n: κεῖθεν is ἐκεῖθεν ‘from there’. πλαγχθέντες is the aorist passive participle of πλάζω ‘drive off course’. ἱκάνομεν is ‘we came’, the imperfect (the same form can be present), and ἐνθάδε is ‘here’. νυκτός is a genitive of time, ‘by night’.

sentences.t:
σπουδῇ δ’ ἐς λιμένα προερέσσαμεν, οὐδέ τις ἡμῖν
δόρπου μνῆστις ἔην, μάλα περ χατέουσιν ἑλέσθαι,
ἀλλ’ αὔτως ἀποβάντες ἐκείμεθα νηὸς ἅπαντες.
sentences.l:
In haste into the harbour we rowed on, and not any for us
thought of supper was there, though greatly needing to take it,
but just as we were, having stepped off the ship, we lay down, all of us.
sentences.i: In haste we rowed on into the harbour, and not one of us gave any thought to supper, though we badly needed to take it, but just as we were we stepped off the ship and lay down, every one of us.
sentences.n: σπουδῇ is ‘in haste’, and προερέσσαμεν is the aorist of προερέσσω ‘row forward’. οὐδέ τις ἡμῖν … μνῆστις ἔην is ‘there was not to us any thought’: μνῆστις is ‘remembrance, thought’ and ἔην is ἦν. χατέουσιν is a dative plural participle of χατέω ‘need, long for’, agreeing with ἡμῖν, and μάλα περ gives it concessive force, ‘though badly needing’, with ἑλέσθαι ‘to take (food)’. αὔτως is ‘just so, as we were’. ἀποβάντες is ‘having stepped off’, with νηός a genitive of separation, and ἐκείμεθα is ‘we lay’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἐμὲ μὲν γλυκὺς ὕπνος ἐπήλυθε κεκμηῶτα,
οἱ δὲ χρήματ’ ἐμὰ γλαφυρῆς ἐκ νηὸς ἑλόντες
κάτθεσαν, ἔνθα περ αὐτὸς ἐπὶ ψαμάθοισιν ἐκείμην.
sentences.l:
then me indeed sweet sleep came upon, worn out,
but they my goods out of the hollow ship having taken
set down, where I myself on the sands was lying.
sentences.i: Then sweet sleep came upon me, worn out as I was; and they took my goods out of the hollow ship and set them down where I myself lay on the sand.
sentences.n: Line 282 is a stock verse for a man overcome by sleep from exhaustion. ἐμὲ μὲν … οἱ δέ sets the sleeper against the Phoenicians. ἐπήλυθε is the aorist of ἐπέρχομαι ‘come upon’, and κεκμηῶτα is the perfect participle of κάμνω ‘be worn out’. γλαφυρῆς ἐκ νηός is ‘out of the hollow ship’. ἑλόντες is the aorist participle of αἱρέω, ‘having taken’, and κάτθεσαν is κατέθεσαν ‘set down’. ἔνθα περ is ‘just where’, and ψαμάθοισιν is the dative plural of ψάμαθος ‘sand’, with the ending -οισιν.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐς Σιδονίην εὖ ναιομένην ἀναβάντες
ᾤχοντ’·
sentences.l:
and they to Sidonia, well-inhabited, having gone aboard,
were gone;
sentences.i: and they went aboard and were gone, to well-peopled Sidon;
sentences.n: Σιδονίην is the land of Sidon, the Phoenician city, and εὖ ναιομένην is ‘well-inhabited’, the passive participle of ναίω ‘dwell’. ἀναβάντες is ‘having gone up’, here on board their ship. ᾤχοντ’ is ᾤχοντο, the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘be gone’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 286.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ λιπόμην ἀκαχήμενος ἦτορ.
sentences.l: but I was left behind, grieved in heart.”
sentences.i: but I was left behind, grieved at heart.”
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is ‘but’, and λιπόμην is the aorist passive-sense middle of λείπω, ‘I was left behind’, without augment. ἀκαχήμενος is the perfect participle of ἀχέω ‘grieve’, with ἦτορ an accusative of respect, ‘grieved as to the heart’. The tale ends with the traveller alone on the shore, and the speech with it.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, μείδησεν δὲ θεὰ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη,
χειρί τέ μιν κατέρεξε·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and smiled the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena,
and with her hand stroked him;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, smiled and stroked him with her hand;
sentences.n: The speech is over, and Athena reacts. ὣς φάτο is ‘so he spoke’, said of Odysseus, and μείδησεν is the aorist of μειδάω ‘smile’. χειρί τέ μιν κατέρεξε is ‘and stroked him with her hand’, with κατέρεξε the aorist of καταρρέζω ‘stroke, caress’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 288, and the change of shape follows.

sentences.t:
δέμας δ’ ἤϊκτο γυναικὶ
καλῇ τε μεγάλῃ τε καὶ ἀγλαὰ ἔργα ἰδυίῃ·
sentences.l:
and in body she was likened to a woman,
fair and tall and knowing splendid works;
sentences.i: and she took the likeness of a woman, fair and tall and skilled in splendid handiwork;
sentences.n: δέμας is an accusative of respect, ‘in body’, and ἤϊκτο is the pluperfect of ἔοικα, ‘she had become like’, with γυναικί the dative ‘to a woman’. καλῇ τε μεγάλῃ τε are two more datives, ‘fair and tall’. ἀγλαὰ ἔργα ἰδυίῃ is ‘skilled in splendid works’: ἰδυίῃ is the feminine dative of the perfect participle of οἶδα, ‘knowing’, and the ‘splendid works’ are usually understood as a woman’s crafts, above all weaving. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 289.

sentences.t: καί μιν φωνήσασ’ ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l: and, lifting her voice, to him winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: and, raising her voice, she spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: The speech formula of 227 and 253 comes a third time, now with the feminine participle φωνήσασ’ (φωνήσασα, elided), because Athena is speaking; μιν is ‘him’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
κερδαλέος κ’ εἴη καὶ ἐπίκλοπος ὅς σε παρέλθοι
ἐν πάντεσσι δόλοισι, καὶ εἰ θεὸς ἀντιάσειε.
sentences.l:
“Gainful would he be, and thievish, whoever should get past you
in all tricks, even if a god should meet you.
sentences.i: “He would have to be shrewd and a trickster, whoever could get the better of you in every kind of trick, even if a god were to meet you.
sentences.n: Athena speaks as herself, and she begins with praise. κ’ is κε(ν), which makes the optative εἴη a potential: ‘he would have to be’. κερδαλέος ‘gainful, shrewd’ comes from κέρδος ‘gain, cunning’, and ἐπίκλοπος is ‘thievish, sly’. ὅς σε παρέλθοι is ‘whoever should get past you’, an aorist optative of παρέρχομαι, here ‘outdo, get the better of’. καὶ εἰ θεὸς ἀντιάσειε is ‘even if a god should meet you’, with ἀντιάσειε the aorist optative of ἀντιάω ‘meet, encounter’. ἐν πάντεσσι δόλοισι is ‘in all tricks’, a dative plural with -εσσι.

sentences.t:
σχέτλιε, ποικιλομῆτα, δόλων ἆτ’, οὐκ ἄρ’ ἔμελλες,
οὐδ’ ἐν σῇ περ ἐὼν γαίῃ, λήξειν ἀπατάων
μύθων τε κλοπίων, οἵ τοι πεδόθεν φίλοι εἰσίν.
sentences.l:
Cruel one, of many-colored cunning, insatiate of tricks, you were not, then, going,
even in your own land being, to cease from deceits
and thievish tales, which to you from the ground up are dear.
sentences.i: You cruel man, full of shifting cunning, never able to get enough of tricks, so you were not, after all, going to leave off deceits even in your own land, nor the sly tales that are dear to you to the very roots.
sentences.n: Athena’s tone is that of a fond reproach, in three vocatives. σχέτλιε is ‘cruel one’ in the house rendering; the Greek word means something nearer ‘hard, headstrong, one who will stop at nothing’, and here it is said with affection. ποικιλομῆτα is ‘of many-colored cunning’ (ποικίλος ‘many-colored’, μῆτις ‘cunning’), and δόλων ἆτ’ is read as ‘insatiate of tricks’, the vocative of ἆτος with the genitive δόλων. οὐκ ἄρ’ ἔμελλες with the future infinitive λήξειν is ‘you were not, after all, going to cease’, and λήγω takes the genitive ἀπατάων ‘deceits’. οὐδ’ … περ ἐών is ‘not even being’. μύθων … κλοπίων is ‘thievish tales’, from κλοπή ‘theft’. πεδόθεν is ‘from the ground’, so ‘to the very roots’. Her speech accuses him of lying and admires him for it.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε, μηκέτι ταῦτα λεγώμεθα, εἰδότες ἄμφω
κέρδε’, ἐπεὶ σὺ μέν ἐσσι βροτῶν ὄχ’ ἄριστος ἁπάντων
βουλῇ καὶ μύθοισιν, ἐγὼ δ’ ἐν πᾶσι θεοῖσι
μήτι τε κλέομαι καὶ κέρδεσιν·
sentences.l:
But come, no longer let us speak of these things, both knowing
cunning-ways, since you are by far the best of mortals, all of them,
in counsel and in speeches, and I among all the gods
am famed for cunning and for cunning-ways;
sentences.i: But come, let us speak no more of this, both of us knowing cunning ways, since you are by far the best of all mortals in counsel and in speech, and I am famed among all the gods for cunning and for cunning ways;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, and μηκέτι ταῦτα λεγώμεθα ‘let us no longer speak of these things’ is a hortative subjunctive of λέγω. εἰδότες ἄμφω is ‘both knowing’, the perfect participle of οἶδα, with κέρδε’ (κέρδεα) ‘cunning ways’ as the object. ὄχ’ is ὄχα ‘by far’ with the superlative ἄριστος. βουλῇ is ‘counsel’ and μύθοισιν ‘speeches’, a dative plural in -οισιν. κλέομαι is ‘I am famed’, a passive form, and μήτι is the dative of μῆτις ‘cunning’. The line sets the two of them side by side, best of mortals and best of gods at the same skill. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 299.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ σύ γ’ ἔγνως
Παλλάδ’ Ἀθηναίην, κούρην Διός, ἥ τέ τοι αἰεὶ
ἐν πάντεσσι πόνοισι παρίσταμαι ἠδὲ φυλάσσω,
sentences.l:
and you did not even recognise
Pallas Athena, daughter of Zeus, who to you always
in all toils stand by and guard,
sentences.i: and you did not even recognise Pallas Athena, daughter of Zeus, who always stand by you in all your toils and guard you,
sentences.n: ἔγνως is the aorist of γιγνώσκω ‘recognise’. The object, Παλλάδ’ Ἀθηναίην κούρην Διός, is the accusative of a name, but the relative ἥ τέ τοι agrees with it while the verbs παρίσταμαι ‘I stand beside’ and φυλάσσω ‘I guard’ are in the first person, because she is naming herself: ‘Athena, who am the one who stands by you’. τε in ἥ τέ marks something always true, and ἐν πάντεσσι πόνοισι is ‘in all toils’. The unit stops at a comma, since the sentence runs to line 310.

sentences.t:
καὶ δέ σε Φαιήκεσσι φίλον πάντεσσιν ἔθηκα,
νῦν αὖ δεῦρ’ ἱκόμην, ἵνα τοι σὺν μῆτιν ὑφήνω
χρήματά τε κρύψω, ὅσα τοι Φαίηκες ἀγαυοὶ
ὤπασαν οἴκαδ’ ἰόντι ἐμῇ βουλῇ τε νόῳ τε,
sentences.l:
and also you to the Phaeacians dear, all of them, I made,
and now again here I have come, so that with you a plan I may weave
and the goods hide, as many as to you the Phaeacians, noble ones,
gave as you went home, by my counsel and my mind,
sentences.i: I made you dear to all the Phaeacians, and now I have come here again so that I may weave a plan with you and hide the goods, all that the noble Phaeacians gave you when you set out for home, by my counsel and my mind,
sentences.n: καὶ δέ σε … ἔθηκα is ‘and I made you’, with φίλον ‘dear’ as a predicate; ἔθηκα is the aorist of τίθημι. νῦν αὖ δεῦρ’ ἱκόμην is ‘now again I have come here’. ἵνα takes the aorist subjunctives ὑφήνω ‘I may weave’ (from ὑφαίνω), κρύψω ‘I may hide’ and, in the next line, εἴπω ‘I may tell’; μῆτιν ὑφήνω ‘weave a plan’ is the same image as weaving a trick. τοι σύν is ‘with you’, the preposition standing after its pronoun. ὅσα … ὤπασαν is ‘all that they gave’, with ὤπασαν the aorist of ὀπάζω. οἴκαδ’ ἰόντι is ‘as you went home’. ἐμῇ βουλῇ τε νόῳ τε is ‘by my counsel and my mind’, a dative of means. The unit stops at a comma because the purpose clause goes on.

sentences.t:
εἴπω θ’ ὅσσα τοι αἶσα δόμοις ἔνι ποιητοῖσι
κήδε’ ἀνασχέσθαι·
sentences.l:
and tell as many as for you fate in the well-built house
sorrows to endure;
sentences.i: and tell you how many sorrows it is your portion to endure in your well-built house;
sentences.n: εἴπω θ’ is the third of the aorist subjunctives under ἵνα (303), ‘and that I may tell you’. ὅσσα … κήδε’ ἀνασχέσθαι is ‘how many sorrows … to endure’: κήδεα ‘sorrows’, and ἀνασχέσθαι the aorist middle infinitive of ἀνέχω ‘hold up, endure’. αἶσα is ‘allotted portion’, so ‘as many as are your portion’. δόμοις ἔνι ποιητοῖσι is ‘in the well-built house’, with ἔνι for ἐν and ποιητός ‘made, well-built’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 307.

sentences.t:
σὺ δὲ τετλάμεναι καὶ ἀνάγκῃ,
μηδέ τῳ ἐκφάσθαι μήτ’ ἀνδρῶν μήτε γυναικῶν,
πάντων, οὕνεκ’ ἄρ’ ἦλθες ἀλώμενος, ἀλλὰ σιωπῇ
πάσχειν ἄλγεα πολλά, βίας ὑποδέγμενος ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.l:
but you, to endure, even under compulsion,
and to no one to disclose, neither of men nor of women,
of all, that you came wandering, but in silence
to suffer many pains, the violence of men submitting to.”
sentences.i: but you must endure, even under compulsion, and tell no one, man or woman, that you came wandering, but in silence suffer many pains, submitting to the violence of men.”
sentences.n: The three infinitives τετλάμεναι, ἐκφάσθαι and πάσχειν stand in place of commands: ‘you must endure … not tell … suffer’. τετλάμεναι is the perfect infinitive of τλάω ‘endure’, with the epic ending -μεναι, and καὶ ἀνάγκῃ is ‘even under compulsion’. μηδέ τῳ ἐκφάσθαι is ‘and not to tell anyone’: τῳ is τινί, and ἐκφάσθαι the middle infinitive of ἐκφημί ‘speak out’, with μήτ’ ἀνδρῶν μήτε γυναικῶν ‘neither of men nor of women’ and πάντων ‘of all’. οὕνεκ’ ἄρ’ ἦλθες ἀλώμενος is ‘that you came wandering’, with οὕνεκα here meaning ‘that’. ὑποδέγμενος is the participle of ὑποδέχομαι (a shortened form), ‘submitting to’, and βίας ἀνδρῶν is ‘the violence of men’. Her speech ends at the full stop.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to her:
sentences.n: A whole-line reply-formula. τὴν δ’ is ‘her’, ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’, and προσέφη ‘said to’, the aorist of πρόσφημι. πολύμητις ‘many-wiled’ is the epithet of Odysseus built on πολύς and μῆτις ‘cunning’, the very quality Athena has just praised in him.

sentences.t:
ἀργαλέον σε, θεά, γνῶναι βροτῷ ἀντιάσαντι,
καὶ μάλ’ ἐπισταμένῳ·
sentences.l:
“Hard it is you, goddess, to know, for a mortal meeting you,
even one who knows very well;
sentences.i: “It is hard, goddess, for a mortal who meets you to know you, even one who knows a great deal;
sentences.n: Odysseus answers at once by accepting who she is. ἀργαλέον is the neuter of ἀργαλέος ‘hard, difficult’, with the infinitive γνῶναι as its subject, and σε is the object of γνῶναι. βροτῷ ἀντιάσαντι is ‘for a mortal who meets (you)’: the aorist participle of ἀντιάω, the verb of 292. καὶ μάλ’ ἐπισταμένῳ is ‘even for one who knows very well’, the participle of ἐπίσταμαι ‘understand’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 313.

sentences.t: σὲ γὰρ αὐτὴν παντὶ ἐΐσκεις.
sentences.l: for yourself to everyone you liken.
sentences.i: for you liken yourself to everyone.
sentences.n: σὲ … αὐτήν is ‘yourself’, the object of ἐΐσκεις, ‘you make like’ (ἐΐσκω), and παντί is ‘to everyone’: she can take any shape. γάρ explains the difficulty named in the line before.

sentences.t:
τοῦτο δ’ ἐγὼν εὖ οἶδ’, ὅτι μοι πάρος ἠπίη ἦσθα,
ἧος ἐνὶ Τροίῃ πολεμίζομεν υἷες Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
But this I well know, that to me before kindly you were,
while in Troy we fought, the sons of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: But this I know well, that you were kind to me before, while we, the sons of the Achaeans, fought at Troy.
sentences.n: τοῦτο δ’ ἐγὼν εὖ οἶδ’ is ‘and this I know well’, with ἐγών the form of ἐγώ before a vowel. ὅτι introduces what he knows: μοι πάρος ἠπίη ἦσθα, ‘formerly you were kindly to me’, with ἠπίη the feminine of ἤπιος ‘kindly’ and ἦσθα the second person of εἰμί. ἧος is ‘while’ (Attic ἕως), and πολεμίζομεν is ‘we were fighting’. υἷες Ἀχαιῶν is ‘the sons of the Achaeans’, with υἷες the epic plural of υἱός.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ Πριάμοιο πόλιν διεπέρσαμεν αἰπήν,
βῆμεν δ’ ἐν νήεσσι, θεὸς δ’ ἐκέδασσεν Ἀχαιούς,
οὔ σέ γ’ ἔπειτα ἴδον, κούρη Διός, οὐδ’ ἐνόησα
νηὸς ἐμῆς ἐπιβᾶσαν, ὅπως τί μοι ἄλγος ἀλάλκοις.
sentences.l:
but when Priam’s city we had utterly sacked, the steep one,
and we went aboard the ships, and a god scattered the Achaeans,
not you thereafter did I see, daughter of Zeus, nor did I notice
you boarding my ship, so that some pain you might ward off for me.
sentences.i: But when we had utterly sacked Priam’s steep city, and had gone aboard our ships, and a god scattered the Achaeans, I did not see you after that, daughter of Zeus, nor notice you coming aboard my ship to ward off some pain for me.
sentences.n: The sentence has a long opening and only then its main verbs. Πριάμοιο is a genitive in -οιο, and αἰπήν ‘steep’ is placed after πόλιν. διεπέρσαμεν is the aorist of διαπέρθω ‘sack utterly’, and βῆμεν is ἐβήμεν, ‘we went’. θεὸς δ’ ἐκέδασσεν Ἀχαιούς is ‘a god scattered the Achaeans’, with ἐκέδασσεν the aorist of κεδάννυμι. οὔ σέ γ’ ἔπειτα ἴδον has ἴδον for εἶδον, ‘I saw’, and ἐνόησα is ‘I noticed’. ἐπιβᾶσαν is the aorist participle of ἐπιβαίνω ‘step on, board’, agreeing with σέ, and it takes the genitive νηὸς ἐμῆς. ὅπως τί μοι ἄλγος ἀλάλκοις is ‘so that you might ward off some pain for me’, with ἀλάλκοις the aorist optative of ἀλαλκεῖν ‘ward off’, the aorist of ἀλέξω. His charge is that she vanished after the war.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ αἰεὶ φρεσὶν ᾗσιν ἔχων δεδαϊγμένον ἦτορ
ἠλώμην, ἧός με θεοὶ κακότητος ἔλυσαν·
sentences.l:
but always in my own mind holding a heart torn apart
I wandered, until the gods released me from misery;
sentences.i: but I wandered always with a heart torn apart within me, until the gods released me from my misery;
sentences.n: ἠλώμην is the imperfect of ἀλάομαι ‘wander’, with a long augment. φρεσὶν ᾗσιν is ‘in my own mind’: ᾗσιν is the possessive ‘own’, which here refers to the speaker, with the dative plural -ῃσιν. δεδαϊγμένον ἦτορ is ‘a heart torn apart’, the perfect passive participle of δαΐζω ‘tear apart’. ἧός is ‘until’, and κακότητος is a genitive of separation after ἔλυσαν ‘released’, with κακότης ‘misery’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in line 321.

sentences.t:
πρίν γ’ ὅτε Φαιήκων ἀνδρῶν ἐν πίονι δήμῳ
θάρσυνάς τε ἔπεσσι καὶ ἐς πόλιν ἤγαγες αὐτή.
sentences.l:
until in the rich land of the Phaeacian men
you heartened me with words and into the city led me, yourself.
sentences.i: until, in the rich land of the Phaeacians, you heartened me with words and led me to their city yourself.
sentences.n: πρίν γ’ ὅτε is ‘until the time when’. πίονι δήμῳ is ‘the rich land’, from πίων ‘rich, fat’ and δῆμος ‘land, district’. θάρσυνας is the aorist of θαρσύνω ‘hearten’, without augment, and ἔπεσσι is the dative plural of ἔπος ‘word’. ἤγαγες is the aorist of ἄγω ‘lead’, and αὐτή ‘yourself’ stresses that she led him in person.

sentences.t:
νῦν δέ σε πρὸς πατρὸς γουνάζομαι—οὐ γὰρ ὀΐω
ἥκειν εἰς Ἰθάκην εὐδείελον, ἀλλά τιν’ ἄλλην
γαῖαν ἀναστρέφομαι·
sentences.i: And now I entreat you in the name of your father — for I do not think I have come to clear-seen Ithaca, but I am going about some other land;
sentences.n: The speech turns to his doubt, which is that the name Ithaca may be a trick. γουνάζομαι is ‘I entreat’, from γόνυ ‘knee’, the suppliant’s gesture, and πρὸς πατρός is ‘in the name of your father’, Zeus. The dash opens a parenthesis: οὐ γὰρ ὀΐω ἥκειν is ‘for I do not think that I have come’, with ὀΐω the present of ὀΐομαι ‘think, suppose’. εὐδείελον is ‘clear-seen’ (see 234). ἀναστρέφομαι is ‘I turn about in’, and takes the accusative γαῖαν. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 326.

sentences.t:
σὲ δὲ κερτομέουσαν ὀΐω
ταῦτ’ ἀγορευέμεναι, ἵν’ ἐμὰς φρένας ἠπεροπεύσῃς—
εἰπέ μοι εἰ ἐτεόν γε φίλην ἐς πατρίδ’ ἱκάνω.
sentences.l:
and you mocking I think
to be saying these things, so that you may deceive my mind—
tell me if truly to my dear fatherland I have come.”
sentences.i: I think you are saying this in mockery, to deceive my mind — tell me whether I have truly come to my dear fatherland.”
sentences.n: σὲ δὲ κερτομέουσαν ὀΐω is ‘and I think you are mocking’: κερτομέουσαν is the feminine accusative participle of κερτομέω ‘mock, taunt’, and ταῦτ’ ἀγορευέμεναι ‘to be saying these things’ has the epic infinitive in -έμεναι. ἵνα with the aorist subjunctive ἠπεροπεύσῃς ‘you may deceive’ gives the purpose, and ἐμὰς φρένας is ‘my wits’. The second dash closes the parenthesis begun at 324. εἰπέ μοι εἰ ἐτεόν γε is ‘tell me if truly’, with ἐτεόν an adverbial accusative, and φίλην ἐς πατρίδ’ ἱκάνω is ‘I come to my dear fatherland’. The speech ends at the full stop.
